entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW), adopted on July 7, 2017, at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, represents a historical milestone in international law aimed at eliminating nuclear weapons and preventing their proliferation. This landmark agreement emerged from a growing global movement advocating for nuclear disarmament, driven by fears of nuclear proliferation and the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of nuclear war. Key players in the negotiation included 122 UN member states, with significant involvement from civil society organizations and anti-nuclear movements, highlighting a collective commitment to global security and human rights.

The treaty, which entered into force on January 22, 2021, establishes a comprehensive legal framework that prohibits the development, testing, production, acquisition, stockpiling, transfer, use, or threat of use of nuclear weapons. It represents the culmination of years of advocacy, building on earlier frameworks such as the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) and the humanitarian initiative that underscored the dire consequences of nuclear armament. The TPNW is anchored in the recognition of the ethical imperative to ensure a safer world free from the existential threat posed by nuclear arms, with over 50 countries ratifying it within its first year of enforcement.
